title: Measured Certainty
text:
Academic writers rarely state conclusions with absolute certainty. Instead, they use modal verbs and qualifying phrases such as 'may indicate' or 'appears to suggest'. These devices allow a writer to report findings while acknowledging that other interpretations remain possible.

Hedging is not merely a matter of style; it reflects an accurate assessment of what the evidence can support. A writer who claims too much risks being refuted by a single contrary study. A writer who hedges appropriately, by contrast, earns trust by showing that the limits of the data have been considered.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what do academic writers use instead of absolute certainty?
What risk does a writer face who claims too much, according to paragraph two?
options: Being refuted by a single contrary study
Losing the reader's interest in the title

questions.text: Why does appropriate hedging earn a writer's trust?
options: It hides the weakness of the evidence
It shows the limits of the data have been considered
It replaces the need for evidence

questions.text: What does the passage imply about hedging?
options: It is a stylistic choice with no connection to evidence
It reflects how well the evidence supports a claim
It should be avoided in academic writing
It is only used in speech

vocabulary.definition: adding a condition that limits how strongly a claim is made
a verb form that shows degrees of certainty, such as 'may' or 'could'
shown to be false by evidence or argument

vocabulary.translation: in a suitable or fitting way
vocabulary.definition: in a way that matches the situation or evidence
